title: Show me one
hook: show me someone ill and happy, in danger and happy: show me a Stoic (Discourses 2.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: count the calm days, every day, then every other, then every third. Did today get a mark? Day four hundred fourteen.

Somebody at a party can explain, in great detail, the whole theory of mindfulness. Five minutes later they're furious at the bartender. We've all been that person, about something. Knowing the words is easy; living them is the hard part. Epictetus' classroom was full of young men who could recite Stoic arguments word for word. One day he stopped being impressed, and asked them for something no amount of reciting could fake. Today: show me one.
screen: `THE WHOLE THEORY OF MINDFULNESS.` → `FURIOUS AT THE BARTENDER.` → `SOMETHING RECITING CAN'T FAKE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter nineteen. It opens with the students showing off a famous puzzle in logic, the kind of thing clever young men loved to argue about. Epictetus lets them talk, and then turns. You can all recite the arguments, he says. So who among you is a Stoic? We call a statue Phidian when it's shaped by Phidias' art. Show me a person shaped by the beliefs they talk about. Then comes the list. Show me someone who is sick, and happy. In danger, and happy. Dying, and happy. Exiled, and happy. Disgraced, and happy. Show me! By the gods, he says, I long to see a Stoic. And then he does something disarming. He lowers the bar. You can't show me one who's finished, he admits. Then show me one who's being shaped, who has started leaning that way. Do an old man a favor. Don't keep from me a sight I've never yet seen. Read that again. Epictetus, the most famous Stoic teacher of his day, says he has never seen a finished Stoic. Not even himself. That's not despair. It's the honesty that keeps the whole thing real. Nobody here is finished. The question is only whether you're being shaped, whether someone watching you on a hard day could see the arguments turning into a person. Not the whole statue. One recognizable line of it.
screen: `CLEVER ARGUMENTS, RECITED.` · `SHAPED LIKE A STATUE BY PHIDIAS.` · `SICK AND HAPPY, EXILED AND HAPPY.` · `SHOW ME ONE BEING SHAPED.` · then, large: `SHOW ME ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Pick one thing you believe about how to live: be patient, be honest, don't panic over what you can't control. Now picture a small hard moment coming today: a delay, a criticism, bad news. Imagine someone watching you in that moment. What would you want them to see? Not perfection. Just one visible line of what you believe. Picture yourself showing it. The bell holds the time.
Show me one. Epictetus' challenge to students who could recite every argument: show me someone sick, in danger or exiled, and still happy, or at least one being shaped that way.
Your line: show me one. In one small hard moment today, be the example, not with words, but with how you handle it. Day four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Many readers of Epictetus judge their practice less by what they know about Stoicism than by how they act on an ordinary hard day.

fork.setup: a student proudly recites a famous logic puzzle. you're Epictetus. what do you ask?
options: show me someone shaped by these beliefs: sick and happy, exiled and happy.
fork.reveal: he asks to see a Stoic in the flesh, then softens it: show me one who's being shaped, a sight he says he's never seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics are people who've mastered their emotions.
what it means: even Epictetus says he's never seen a finished Stoic; what counts is being shaped.
what a scholar hears: 2.19 opens with the 'Master Argument' of Diodorus Cronus, a famous logic puzzle, which makes the turn to living all the sharper.

sources.ref: Discourses 2.19 (the Master Argument; 'show me a Stoic')
